strengths: Addresses an important limitation of amortized Bayesian inference: inaccurate posterior approximation on observations far from the simulation training distribution. Using unlabeled observations for additional training is practically appealing and preserves amortized inference after training.

The Gaussian case study shows substantial improvements over standard neural posterior estimation, including extrapolation beyond the unlabeled training distribution. Experiments vary dimensionality, unlabeled sample size and location, summary networks, and likelihood availability.

An analytic reference posterior permits direct assessment of approximation error. The paper also acknowledges the weaker performance and identifiability limitations associated with jointly learned likelihoods and posteriors.
weaknesses: The evaluation is insufficient for a top-tier conference: every experiment uses the same conjugate, isotropic Gaussian model, whose posterior mean is linear in the observations and whose covariance is constant. Increasing this model to 100 dimensions does not establish robustness for correlated, nonlinear, multimodal, or otherwise challenging posteriors. There are no real-data applications or additional simulator benchmarks; promised future experiments cannot support the present submission.

Proposition 4 is false as stated. A known posterior and prior do not generally uniquely identify the likelihood through constancy of the ratio across parameters. For example, if the true likelihood is independent of the parameter, the posterior equals the prior. Any different normalized likelihood q(x|theta)=r(x) that is also independent of the parameter makes the ratio constant across theta and attains zero self-consistency variance. Exchanging likelihood and posterior in the proof of Proposition 1 therefore does not establish strict properness.

Propositions 1–2 also require stronger support and finiteness assumptions. Constancy over the true posterior's support only establishes proportionality there; an approximate posterior can place additional mass outside that support, invalidating the normalization step in Equation 8. Furthermore, a proposal whose support strictly exceeds the posterior's can encounter undefined log ratios. These issues do not invalidate the full-support Gaussian example, but they undermine the stated general guarantees.

Novelty is limited relative to the authors' cited self-consistency work [34]: the loss already exists, and the principal extension is evaluating it on unlabeled shifted observations. The only experimental baseline is standard NPE. Comparisons with alternative likelihood-informed amortized objectives, relevant robustness methods, and stronger or compute-matched NPE training are needed to establish the extension's significance.

Several claims exceed the evidence. Agreement with the posterior under an assumed model demonstrates reduced approximation error, not correction of model misspecification or reliable uncertainty about real-world parameters. Claims of a 'major breakthrough,' unprecedented robustness, and no major curse of dimensionality are unsupported by this single model family. Likewise, shared population minimizers do not imply an absence of practical accuracy–robustness trade-offs under finite capacity and optimization.

Important reproducibility and statistical details are missing: the self-consistency weight lambda, whether gradients propagate through posterior proposal samples, the number of independent training runs, and the meaning of the plotted error bars. The Gaussian-kernel MMD estimator, bandwidth, and scaling are unspecified; reported values around 15 require clarification because conventional unit-amplitude Gaussian-kernel MMD is bounded by sqrt(2). No implementation link is provided.

The estimated-likelihood setting, which is especially relevant to simulation-based inference, exhibits substantial posterior standard-deviation bias. Together with the acknowledged non-identifiability of joint self-consistency, this leaves a major practical limitation unresolved. Training overhead and sensitivity to the proposal distribution, loss weight, and number of parameter samples are also not evaluated.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of amortized Bayesian inference: inaccurate posterior approximation on observations far from the simulation training distribution. Incorporating unlabeled observations through Bayesian self-consistency is a useful and conceptually simple approach.

The controlled Gaussian experiments show substantial improvements over the tested NPE baseline, including extrapolation beyond the unlabeled training observations. Analytic reference posteriors make these improvements directly assessable.

The experiments investigate several relevant factors: parameter dimension, unlabeled sample size and location, learned likelihoods, and summary networks. The paper also acknowledges that jointly learned likelihoods and posteriors need additional supervision.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims contain substantive errors. Proposition 4 is false in general: if p(x|θ)=p(x), then p(θ|x)=p(θ), and any normalized q(x|θ)=r(x) makes the proposed ratio constant in θ, although r(x) need not equal p(x). Normalizing the likelihood over x does not reproduce the posterior-normalization argument. Proposition 1 also needs an additional support restriction: q can allocate a fraction of its mass proportionally to the true posterior and the remaining mass outside its support, while keeping the ratio constant throughout the posterior support. These issues undermine the stated general strict-properness guarantees, although the latter support issue does not affect the full-support Gaussian example.

The evaluation is restricted to one conjugate, isotropic Gaussian model. Its posterior mean is linear in the observed sample mean and its covariance is constant, making it a particularly favorable extrapolation problem. Increasing the dimension to 100 does not test correlated, multimodal, nonlinear, or otherwise difficult posterior geometry. The manuscript explicitly defers broader benchmarks to future work; those missing experiments are essential for assessing the claimed general robustness.

Novelty beyond the authors' prior self-consistency work [22, 34] is primarily applying the existing loss to unlabeled, shifted observations. The comparison is almost exclusively against standard NPE. There are no empirical comparisons with the robustness methods discussed in related work, alternative likelihood-informed objectives, or stronger extrapolation baselines. The advantage over existing approaches therefore remains unestablished.

Experimental reporting is insufficient for reliable reproduction and interpretation. The self-consistency weight λ is not specified, nor are the handling of gradients through posterior-drawn proposal samples, the number of independent training runs, or the meaning of the plotted error bars. The MMD estimator and kernel bandwidth are also unspecified. Training-time overhead and comparisons at matched computational budgets are absent.

The robustness claims exceed the demonstrated result. Matching the exact posterior under an assumed model establishes approximation fidelity, not that inference is statistically reliable when that model is misspecified. Likewise, common population minimizers do not establish an absence of accuracy–robustness trade-offs under finite model capacity and optimization. Claims of a 'major breakthrough' and 'no major curse of dimensionality' are unsupported by this case study.

The learned-likelihood experiment exposes an important unresolved limitation: posterior standard deviations become substantially overestimated under large shifts, with absolute errors exceeding those of the baseline at some locations. Improvements in posterior means and MMD therefore do not establish uniformly accurate uncertainty quantification in the setting where the likelihood must itself be learned.

strengths: Addresses an important limitation of amortized Bayesian inference: posterior approximation can deteriorate severely on observations far from the simulation training distribution.

The proposed use of self-consistency losses on unlabeled observations is conceptually simple and preserves amortized inference after training. It does not require ground-truth parameters for the additional observations.

The Gaussian case study shows substantial improvements over standard neural posterior estimation, including extrapolation beyond the unlabeled training distribution. Analytic reference posteriors make these improvements directly assessable.

The experiments examine several useful factors: parameter dimensionality, unlabeled dataset size and location, summary networks, and learned versus analytic likelihoods. The learned-likelihood limitations are acknowledged.
weaknesses: The evaluation is insufficient for the breadth of the claims. All experiments use one conjugate, isotropic Gaussian model whose posterior mean is linear in the observations and whose covariance is constant. Varying its dimensionality does not establish robustness for nonlinear models, correlated or multimodal posteriors, or real applications. The additional experiments promised in the manuscript cannot count as evidence in this submission.

Proposition 4 is false as stated: knowing the posterior and prior does not generally identify the likelihood through constancy of the self-consistency ratio across parameters. For example, if the true likelihood is independent of theta, then the posterior equals the prior. Any normalized alternative q(x|theta)=r(x), also independent of theta, makes the ratio constant across theta and minimizes the variance loss, even when r differs from the true likelihood. Exchanging likelihood and posterior in Proposition 1's proof is invalid because their normalization is over different variables. This does not invalidate the known-likelihood experiments, but it requires correcting the theoretical claims.

The principal loss already appears in the authors' cited prior work [22, 34]; the main extension here is applying it to unlabeled out-of-simulation observations. This is potentially useful, but its significance is not established by comparisons only against standard NPE. Comparisons with amortized variational training using the same available likelihood, relevant robustness methods, and stronger or compute-matched NPE baselines are missing.

The demonstrated robustness concerns agreement with the posterior under the assumed model, not correction of model misspecification or calibrated uncertainty under the real data-generating process. Claims about safe applicability, a 'major breakthrough,' and the absence of a major curse of dimensionality exceed what this experiment establishes. Shared population minimizers also do not rule out practical accuracy–robustness trade-offs under finite capacity and optimization.

Important reproducibility and evaluation details are missing: the self-consistency weight lambda and its selection, whether gradients propagate through posterior samples used in the variance loss, the number of independent training runs and evaluation datasets, the meaning of plotted error bars, and the MMD bandwidth and estimator. Training-time and likelihood-evaluation overheads are not reported.

The practically important learned-likelihood setting retains substantial errors: Figure 3 shows posterior standard-deviation overestimation increasing markedly with the observation shift. There are no ablations over proposal distributions, loss weights, or sampling budgets to characterize stability, and the strict-properness discussion does not establish reliable finite-sample optimization when both densities are learned.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of amortized Bayesian inference: inaccurate posterior approximations on observations poorly represented by training simulations. Applying self-consistency losses to unlabeled observations is a practical extension that preserves fast inference after training.

The reported improvements over standard NPE are substantial. The Gaussian experiments explore dimensionality, unlabeled-data quantity and location, learned likelihoods, and summary networks. The air-traffic example provides useful evidence with real observations and a Stan reference.

The manuscript clearly explains the objective and acknowledges the non-identifiability arising when both likelihood and posterior are learned. Architectural and optimization details in the appendix provide a useful starting point for reproduction.
weaknesses: Proposition 4 is false in general: knowing the posterior and prior does not uniquely determine the likelihood through consistency across parameters. For example, when the true likelihood is independent of θ, the posterior equals the prior. Any alternative normalized likelihood q(x|θ)=r(x), also independent of θ, makes the self-consistency ratio constant across θ and minimizes the loss, even when r differs from the true likelihood. Exchanging posterior and likelihood in the proof of Proposition 1 is therefore invalid.

Proposition 1 also needs an additional support restriction. Constancy on the posterior support only implies that q is proportional to the posterior there; q can assign additional probability outside that support. For example, q=c p(θ|x)+(1−c)r(θ), with r supported outside the posterior support, yields a constant ratio on the posterior support without equaling the posterior. The normalization step in Appendix A.1 incorrectly extends the equality to the entire integration domain. The posterior result is repairable under suitable support and finiteness assumptions, but the stated general guarantees are not established.

The methodological novelty relative to Schmitt et al. (2024) is limited: the self-consistency ratio and variance objective are inherited, with the main extension being their application to unlabeled, out-of-simulation observations. There is no systematic comparison against the prior self-consistency method on simulated observations, or against an amortized reverse-KL objective using the same unlabeled observations and likelihood access. Comparisons only with standard NPE do not establish the advantage of this particular objective.

The evaluation is too narrow for the broad robustness claims. It consists of a conjugate Gaussian model and a five-parameter Gaussian autoregression. The high-dimensional experiment retains a particularly simple posterior structure, and the learned-likelihood experiment exhibits substantial residual variance bias. There are no challenging multimodal or nonlinear simulator benchmarks. Claims of a 'major breakthrough,' unmatched robustness, and no major curse of dimensionality exceed the evidence.

The real-data evaluation mixes observations used by the self-consistency loss with held-out observations: Tables 1–3 average over all 15 countries, while training uses 4, 8, or all 15. Using these observations for unlabeled training is legitimate, but the aggregate results do not isolate generalization to unseen countries. The paper should identify the selected countries, report held-out performance separately, and repeat the country selection.

Important implementation and validation details are missing, including the value or schedule of λ, whether gradients propagate through samples drawn from the current posterior, the definition of plotted error bars and number of repetitions, and Stan convergence diagnostics. No training-time or compute-matched comparison supports the claim of competitive training costs, and the fixed 1,024-simulation budget does not substantiate the assertion that additional simulation cannot resolve baseline failures in acceptable time.

The demonstrated robustness concerns approximation of the posterior under the assumed model, rather than recovery of reliable scientific conclusions under model misspecification. Agreement with Stan does not establish calibration or predictive validity under the real data-generating process. Similarly, shared population-level minimizers do not establish the claimed absence of an accuracy–robustness trade-off with finite data, restricted network capacity, and imperfect optimization.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of amortized Bayesian inference: inaccurate posterior approximations on observations poorly represented by training simulations. Applying self-consistency losses to unlabeled observations is a useful, practical extension.

The reported improvements over standard NPE are substantial. In the air-traffic experiment, posterior mean error for the autoregressive coefficient decreases from 0.152 to 0.030 with eight unlabeled countries, and all reported aggregate metrics improve.

The Gaussian experiments examine parameter dimensionality, unlabeled-data quantity and location, summary networks, and learned likelihoods. Analytic posteriors and Stan provide appropriate reference targets.
weaknesses: Proposition 4 is false as stated: a known posterior and prior do not generally identify the likelihood through constancy of the ratio over parameters. For example, if p(x|θ)=f(x), then p(θ|x)=p(θ); any normalized q(x|θ)=g(x) makes the proposed ratio constant in θ, including g≠f. Normalization over x cannot be substituted for normalization over θ in the proposed proof.

Propositions 1–2 also require stronger support conditions. Constancy on the posterior support permits q to equal c·p there while assigning the remaining probability outside that support. Appendix A.1 incorrectly extends equality on the posterior support to the integral over the entire parameter space. Matching supports and suitable positivity/integrability assumptions would address this issue for the Gaussian examples, but the general theorem is overstated.

The methodological novelty is limited: the self-consistency ratio and variance loss come from prior work [26, 38]. The main extension is evaluating this loss on unlabeled out-of-simulation observations. Its competitiveness is not established against alternative likelihood-based objectives, such as amortized variational inference, or existing robustness approaches.

Evaluation covers only a conjugate Gaussian model and a five-parameter Gaussian autoregression, primarily with tractable likelihoods. Standard NPE with 1,024 simulations is the only substantive learned baseline. There are no simulation-budget curves or matched-compute comparisons supporting the claim that simply generating more training data cannot resolve the problem in acceptable time.

The real-data evaluation mixes countries used for self-consistency training with unseen countries in its aggregate metrics. The M=15 experiment evaluates entirely on observations used by the unsupervised objective. Separate held-out-country results and repeated country selections are needed to establish generalization rather than adaptation to supplied observations.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including the self-consistency weight λ, its selection procedure, differentiation through samples from the current posterior, training repetitions, and the meaning of plotted error bars. The air-traffic setup also lacks sufficient preprocessing and covariate-simulation details, while Stan convergence diagnostics and measured computational costs are absent.

The conclusions exceed the evidence. Agreement with the posterior under the assumed model demonstrates reduced approximation error, not calibrated inference under model misspecification. Population objectives sharing a minimizer do not establish an absence of finite-capacity accuracy–robustness trade-offs. Claims of a 'major breakthrough' and no major dimensionality curse are premature, especially given the residual high-dimensional errors and substantial posterior-scale bias with a learned likelihood.

Figure 4 shows substantial remaining uncertainty-estimation error with a learned likelihood. Claims of a 'major breakthrough,' unmatched robustness, and no major curse of dimensionality exceed this evidence.

The air-traffic results average over all 15 countries, including those used for self-consistency training. The M=15 experiment therefore evaluates entirely on training observations. For M=4 and M=8, separate held-out results, identified country splits, and repeated splits are needed to establish generalization. Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are incomplete: the self-consistency weight λ, treatment of gradients through posterior proposal samples, replication counts and error-bar definitions, and Stan convergence diagnostics are not specified. strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: amortized posterior estimators can fail badly on observations poorly represented by simulator-generated training data. Using unlabeled observations through a self-consistency objective is a useful and straightforward approach.

The Gaussian experiments provide convincing evidence of improvements over the tested NPE baseline, including substantial extrapolation gains, ten independent refits, and ablations over dimensionality, unlabeled-data size, summary networks, and likelihood estimation.
The air-traffic application provides a meaningful real-data comparison against Stan. Table 1 shows substantial reductions in posterior approximation errors across several parameters.
The experiments span analytic models, time series, and images, and the appendices provide substantial architecture and training details.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees contain substantive errors. Proposition 4 is false: if p(x|θ)=r(x), then p(θ|x)=p(θ), and any normalized likelihood q(x|θ)=s(x) independent of θ makes the self-consistency ratio constant over θ, even when s differs from r. Normalizing over x cannot identify the θ-independent proportionality factor separately for each x. Proposition 1 also needs a restriction preventing q from assigning mass outside the posterior support; otherwise q can equal a scaled posterior on that support and place its remaining mass elsewhere while attaining the same minimum. Appendix A implicitly assumes away this possibility.

The claims of robustness without trade-offs exceed the guarantees. Agreement of population minimizers in an unrestricted function class does not establish absence of trade-offs with finite data, shared finite-capacity networks, or imperfect optimization. Nor does it guarantee extrapolation beyond the unlabeled observations. Accurate approximation of a misspecified model's posterior should also be distinguished from calibrated inference about the real data-generating process.

Comparisons are almost entirely against vanilla NPE/NPLE. The paper does not empirically compare against the discussed robustness or adaptation methods, or against amortized variational training using the available likelihood. It also lacks matched-compute comparisons and simulation-budget scaling. Consequently, the results establish improvement over the selected baseline but not competitiveness with strong alternatives.

The most complex experiments do not establish posterior accuracy or calibration. Hodgkin–Huxley evaluation measures posterior predictive mean error, which can improve despite incorrect parameter uncertainty or missing posterior modes. MNIST evaluation is qualitative, without reconstruction metrics, coverage measurements, or a posterior reference. Moreover, its stated observation mechanism is deterministic Gaussian blurring, leaving the probabilistic likelihood and interpretation of posterior uncertainty insufficiently specified.

Evidence for generalization to unseen real observations is limited. Air-traffic metrics aggregate countries used for self-consistency training with held-out countries, and the M=15 setting uses every evaluated country during training. Separate held-out results and repeated country splits are needed to assess the claimed generalization benefit.

The methodological novelty is limited relative to the acknowledged prior self-consistency work: the central ratio and variance objective are inherited, with the main extension being evaluation on unlabeled observations from a different distribution. This could support a valuable empirical contribution, but the missing comparisons and posterior-level validation currently leave that contribution insufficiently established.

Important reproducibility and efficiency details remain missing, including self-consistency weights or schedules for most tasks, whether gradients propagate through proposal samples, and reference MCMC convergence diagnostics. Training-cost comparisons and sensitivity to the proposal distribution and loss weight are also absent, despite their direct relevance to practical robustness.

The air-traffic application demonstrates meaningful improvements against Stan: for example, Table 1 reduces the posterior-mean error for β from 0.153 to 0.031. The appendices provide substantial model and architecture details.

The claims of robustness without trade-offs overstate what population-level minimizer arguments establish. Shared unrestricted optima do not exclude trade-offs under finite network capacity, finite data, or imperfect optimization, and they provide no guarantee of extrapolation beyond both training distributions. Comparisons are limited to standard NPE/NPLE. The variance-based self-consistency objective already comes from prior work, making its application to unlabeled shifted observations the principal novelty. Comparisons with amortized variational training using the same likelihood information, relevant robustness methods, and stronger or compute-matched NPE baselines are needed to establish the significance of this extension. The claim that additional simulations cannot remedy the problem is not supported by simulation-budget scaling experiments.

The harder applications do not establish posterior accuracy or calibration. Hodgkin–Huxley is evaluated primarily through posterior-predictive mean error, which cannot validate parameter uncertainty or posterior dependence. MNIST offers qualitative images without aggregate reconstruction metrics, calibration tests, or a posterior reference. Visually smoother samples and uncertainty maps are insufficient evidence for the broad posterior-correctness claims, particularly when both likelihood and posterior are learned.

The MNIST probabilistic model is insufficiently specified. Appendix H describes deterministic Gaussian blurring without observation noise, implying a singular conditional distribution rather than an ordinary continuous likelihood density. Fitting a full-dimensional likelihood flow therefore needs an explicit noise or dequantization model, or a careful account of the approximation target. This matters directly to the interpretation of the self-consistency ratio.

Important evaluation and reproducibility details remain missing. Air-traffic metrics combine countries used for self-consistency training with unseen countries, obscuring generalization performance. Outside MNIST, self-consistency weights and schedules are not clearly specified; gradient handling through posterior proposal samples is unclear, and training overhead is not systematically compared. These omissions make the practical robustness and efficiency claims difficult to assess.

Applying self-consistency losses to unlabeled target observations is useful and preserves amortized inference after training.

The Gaussian experiments provide clear improvements against an analytic posterior, with ten repeated fits and ablations covering dimensionality, unlabeled dataset size, summary networks, and estimated likelihoods.

The air-traffic application provides encouraging real-data evidence against a Stan reference. For example, Table 1 reports a reduction in posterior-mean error for the autoregressive coefficient from 0.153 to 0.031.
The experiments span several distinct settings, and the appendices provide substantial architecture and training information.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees contain substantive errors. Proposition 4 is false in general: if the true likelihood is independent of the parameters, the posterior equals the prior, and any other normalized likelihood independent of the parameters also makes the self-consistency ratio constant across parameters. Thus, the loss cannot uniquely identify the true likelihood. Exchanging posterior and likelihood in Proposition 1 does not preserve its normalization argument.

Proposition 1 also needs an explicit restriction excluding approximate-posterior mass outside the true posterior's support. Otherwise, an approximation can equal a scaled true posterior on that support and place its remaining mass elsewhere while keeping the ratio constant. Appendix A incorrectly extends an equality established only on the posterior support to the entire normalization integral. The claimed absence of trade-offs additionally concerns unrestricted population optima, not finite-capacity networks trained on finite data.

Evaluation compares almost exclusively against standard NPE/NPLE. There are no empirical comparisons with the discussed robustness or adaptation methods, an amortized variational objective using the same likelihood access, or self-consistency applied only to simulated observations. Simulation-budget and matched-compute comparisons are also missing. Consequently, the advantage of the proposed semi-supervised formulation over credible alternatives is insufficiently established.

The high-dimensional studies do not substantiate accurate, well-calibrated posterior inference. Hodgkin–Huxley evaluation measures posterior predictive mean error, which does not establish parameter-posterior accuracy or uncertainty calibration. MNIST evaluation is qualitative, without quantitative reconstruction metrics, coverage measurements, or a reference posterior. Visually coherent uncertainty maps alone cannot establish correct uncertainty.

The MNIST likelihood is described as deterministic Gaussian blurring, without an explicit observation-noise model. Such a conditional distribution is singular rather than an ordinary density over pixels, leaving the interpretation of the learned likelihood and resulting Bayesian posterior unclear. Moreover, when posterior and likelihood are jointly estimated, self-consistency does not identify their correctness, as the paper itself acknowledges.

The core variance loss comes from prior work; the main methodological novelty is its application to unlabeled target data. Stronger comparisons and evidence are needed to establish the significance of this extension. Reproducibility also remains incomplete: the self-consistency weight and schedule are not consistently specified across experiments, differentiation through proposal samples is unclear, and training overhead is not systematically reported.

For example, if the true likelihood is independent of the parameter, then the posterior equals the prior; any alternative normalized likelihood q(x|theta)=r(x), also independent of theta, makes the proposed ratio constant over theta and attains zero variance. Thus, an incorrect likelihood can minimize the loss even with the exact posterior. The claimed proof by exchanging likelihood and posterior overlooks their different normalization variables.

The other theoretical claims need stronger qualifications. Proposition 1 constrains q only on the posterior support, but its normalization argument implicitly assumes q has no mass outside that support. Proposition 2 also needs conditions ensuring finite log ratios. Moreover, shared population minimizers do not establish the claimed absence of accuracy–robustness trade-offs for finite-capacity networks, finite datasets, or imperfect optimization, and they provide no guarantee of extrapolation beyond the unlabeled training distribution.

The most relevant alternative objective is not adequately controlled. Appendix F.1 trains the variational baseline on simulated data with a Gaussian encoder, whereas NPE+SC uses unlabeled real observations and a more expressive flow. A comparison against amortized reverse-KL/ELBO training on the same unlabeled observations, using the same posterior architecture and supervised anchor, is needed to isolate the benefit of the self-consistency objective. The objective itself is inherited from prior work, making this comparison especially important.

The high-dimensional experiments do not substantiate accurate or calibrated posterior inference. Hodgkin–Huxley is assessed through posterior predictive mean error, which can improve despite incorrect parameter uncertainty or missing posterior modes. MNIST provides qualitative reconstructions and uncertainty maps without quantitative reconstruction metrics, coverage tests, or a posterior reference. Visually coherent variance maps are not evidence of calibration.

The MNIST probabilistic formulation is incomplete. The stated observation mechanism applies a fixed Gaussian blur without specifying random observation noise, yielding a deterministic conditional distribution rather than an ordinary likelihood density on the image space. Training a continuous likelihood flow and interpreting its variance maps as Bayesian uncertainty therefore require an explicit noise model or a justification of the surrogate target.

Table 1 contains reporting inconsistencies that require correction. It labels entries as mean absolute errors with standard errors across 15 countries, but reports values such as 0.003 ± 0.009 and 0.006 ± 0.026. For nonnegative observations, the usual sample standard error cannot exceed their sample mean. These entries suggest that either the metric, uncertainty label, or computation differs from the description.

Generalization and computational evidence remain incomplete. The strongest additional air-traffic comparisons evaluate all 15 countries after using those same countries for self-consistency training; these demonstrate adaptation rather than held-out generalization. Results should separately quantify unseen-country performance. Training overhead and additional likelihood evaluations are also not systematically reported, particularly for the ODE-based task.

The reproducibility statement points to code in the abstract, but the supplied manuscript ends that sentence at 'The code is available at' without a URL. Important implementation choices, including whether gradients propagate through posterior samples used in the variance loss, are not clearly specified.

Applying self-consistency losses to unlabeled observations is a useful extension of prior work that preserves fast inference after training.

The Gaussian experiments provide substantial positive evidence, including analytic posterior comparisons, 10 repeated fits, and ablations over dimensionality, unlabeled sample size, summary networks, and likelihood estimation.

The air-traffic study shows substantial improvements against Stan. The appendices include comparisons with domain-adaptation methods, online NPE, a VAE, and the earlier simulation-only self-consistency method, alongside considerable architectural detail.

Any alternative normalized likelihood q(x|θ)=r(x), independent of θ, makes the proposed ratio constant in θ and achieves zero variance, even when r(x) differs from p(x). The theoretical conclusions exceed what the arguments establish. The claims that reducing log-ratio variance reduces KL divergence also require qualifications beyond agreement at the global optimum.

The MNIST probabilistic model is underspecified. Appendix I describes observations produced by a fixed deterministic Gaussian blur, without an explicit random observation-noise model. Such a simulator has a singular conditional distribution, rather than the ordinary likelihood density assumed by the flow-based objective. The paper needs to specify any noise or dequantization and explain the posterior being targeted. Jointly learning likelihood and posterior also lacks the identification guarantee, as the authors acknowledge.

The baseline comparisons do not isolate the proposed loss sufficiently. The VAE uses a different, more restrictive posterior family and is described as training on simulations, whereas the proposed method additionally accesses real observations. A matched expressive posterior trained with an ELBO on the same unlabeled observations would better distinguish the benefit of self-consistency from access to likelihood information and target-domain data. Strong comparisons on the high-dimensional tasks are also missing.

The air-traffic generalization evidence mixes observations used for self-consistency training with unseen countries. Table 2 evaluates all 15 countries after using all 15 during training; Table 1 averages adapted and held-out countries together. Separate held-out results and repeated country splits are needed to assess generalization reliably.

Some reported statistics require correction or explanation. Table 1 labels entries as mean absolute errors with standard errors across countries, yet reports values such as 0.003 ± 0.009. For nonnegative observations, the conventional sample standard error cannot exceed their sample mean. This suggests that either the metric or uncertainty calculation is mislabeled. Reproducibility is also weakened by the absent code URL despite the reproducibility statement claiming one is provided.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: amortized posterior estimators can fail badly on observations poorly represented by their simulation training distribution. Applying self-consistency losses to unlabeled observations is a useful and straightforward extension of existing methods.

The normal-model experiments provide substantial positive evidence, including comparisons with analytic posteriors, ten independent refits, and ablations over dimensionality, unlabeled sample size, summary networks, and likelihood estimation.

The air-traffic application demonstrates meaningful improvements against Stan references. Appendix F.1 strengthens the evaluation by including online NPE, a VAE baseline, and self-consistency trained on simulated observations.

The method preserves the inference architecture and requires no additional correction at deployment. Experiments with time series and images demonstrate potential applicability beyond low-dimensional examples.
weaknesses: Proposition 4 is false as stated: constancy across parameters does not identify a likelihood normalized across observations. For example, if p(x|θ)=r(x), then p(θ|x)=p(θ). Any alternative normalized likelihood q(x|θ)=s(x) makes the proposed ratio equal s(x), constant in θ, while generally differing from r(x). Exchanging likelihood and posterior therefore does not establish strict properness. Proposition 1 also needs an explicit support restriction on q: proportionality on the posterior support does not preclude q assigning additional mass outside it.

The theoretical conclusions exceed what identification of a global optimum establishes. A common unrestricted optimum does not eliminate trade-offs under finite network capacity, learned summaries, finite data, or imperfect optimization. Likewise, sharing the KL minimizer does not imply that reducing the variance loss reduces KL throughout training. No result guarantees generalization to observations outside both training distributions.

The higher-dimensional experiments do not substantiate accurate, calibrated posterior inference. Hodgkin–Huxley is evaluated through posterior predictive fit rather than parameter-posterior accuracy or uncertainty calibration. MNIST provides qualitative reconstructions and uncertainty maps without quantitative reconstruction metrics, coverage, or posterior references. Visually coherent uncertainty is insufficient evidence of calibration, especially when jointly estimated likelihoods and posteriors can be self-consistent yet incorrect.

The MNIST likelihood is underspecified. Appendix I describes a fixed deterministic Gaussian blur without additive observation noise, which induces a singular conditional distribution rather than the ordinary conditional density assumed by likelihood-flow training. The manuscript needs to specify any noise or dequantization and explain how the resulting inference target relates to its theoretical framework.

The comparisons do not isolate the benefit of the particular self-consistency objective sufficiently. The VAE baseline uses a restricted Gaussian encoder and simulated training observations, whereas the proposed method uses expressive flows and real observations. An equally expressive amortized variational baseline trained on the same unlabeled observations with the same known likelihood would be more informative. The strongest air-traffic comparison uses all 15 evaluated countries during training; results for previously unseen countries should be reported separately.

The underlying variance loss is inherited from prior work, making the principal contribution its semi-supervised application. Stronger evaluation is needed to establish this extension at a top-tier venue, particularly given the theoretical errors. Reproducibility is also incomplete: the abstract's promised code link is absent, and implementation details such as gradient handling through proposal samples are unclear.
